voice_event.text:
He is God's own Word - the Logos, through whom all things were made - come in flesh. Clement, one of our first teachers, opened with him as the New Song: “See the power of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts. And those who were like the dead, with no share in the true life, have come to life again, simply by listening to this song. It also arranged the universe in melodious order. It tuned the discord of the elements into harmonious arrangement, so that the whole world might become harmony.”

He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right. By that we meant that his own life is opened to us and shared. His death is the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection - the anastasis - is unbreakable life let loose in human flesh. From the beginning we worshiped him as God's own Word and baptized into Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The precise wording was the work of our last years: when Arius taught that the Son was the first and highest creature, the council at Nicaea answered with homoousios - of one substance with the Father. What we hold is the worship, the baptismal formula, and the fought-for conviction that only God can join us to God.

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text:
Athanasius put it plainest: “For he was made man, so that we might be made God...”

He entered what was broken to heal it from within. His death was the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection let unbreakable life loose in human flesh. That is what he did: he opened God's own life to us, so that we might share it.

We can also tell you a story Clement handed down as true tradition, because it shows what following him meant. The apostle John had left a young man in a bishop's care. The bishop grew careless. The young man fell in with a gang and became their chief. Years later, John came back and asked for him. When he learned what had happened, the old man rode out into the mountains. The bandits took him. He called the young man by name. The young man tried to run. John ran after him, calling him back - not to punishment, but to restoration. The cost was real: the young man had to walk the long road back, and John walked it with him. That story stayed with us because it showed the pattern: what was lost could be brought back, but the bringing back was never cheap.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text:
Logikos - made for the Word. Every being that could know God was logikos, able to turn toward him. The word comes from Logos, the Word himself, through whom all things were made.

One of our teachers built this into a wider view of the cosmos - that rational natures existed before the world began, and fell into bodies. That view is contested, and so is whether it was his own. What stayed firm among us was the simpler claim: we were made for the Word, and the image of God in us - the eikon - is what makes knowing him possible.

We used logikos to say something about direction. A soul is not logikos because it is clever. It is logikos because it was made to know the one who made it. That capacity can be damaged by the fall, but never destroyed. Formation is what turns it back toward its purpose.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text:
We believed it because we believed the witnesses. The apostles who had run when he was arrested went on teaching afterward, at the cost of their own lives - and our teacher Origen argued that no invented story produces courage like that. What they handed down to us was not only a claim about a past event, but a present sharing in his life. We received baptism, the bread and cup, the scriptures read aloud, and the rule of faith as the apostles' deposit, handed down. We did not invent them in Alexandria - we kept what had been given.

And we believed it because of what it did. He meant love for the Holy Word, and for the teacher who showed him the Word. Formation was not agreement with claims - it was the soul turned toward God and changed by him. We saw it happen. Scripture read at depth was the instrument. The water and the table were the turning points. The lives remade were the evidence.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text:
Clement, one of our first teachers, lived this out in how he taught. That is what Clement himself became: a teacher whose wisdom was visible in how he loved both truth and the people he taught.

He defended marriage against those who despised it. That was not popular with everyone. But it showed the shape of his soul: he saw God at work everywhere, even outside our own walls.

What made him our kind of teacher was that he believed the soul could grow. Faith was the foundation, not the ceiling. And the growing happened through patient work - Scripture read at depth, a life turned step by step, love as the fruit rather than the start.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text:
We would want you to understand that the door stood open wider than the surviving books make it look.

What survives is mostly the teachers' writings - arguments, commentaries, lectures to the lettered few. That makes us sound like a school for philosophers. We were not only that. The school was real, and its formation went deep. But the whole community gathered around the water and the table: baptism, the bread and cup, the scriptures read aloud. Those reached everyone, whether they could read or not.

The problem is this: the teachers wrote books, and books survived. The majority who could not read left almost nothing. The villages up the river appear in our record only when their bishop went out to them. So the record makes it look as though formation belonged only to the school. It did not. The school's depth-formation was for the few. The whole community's formation was real too, and it ran through different channels.

Athanasius names books outside what became the canon - Wisdom, the Teaching of the Apostles, the Shepherd - appointed by the fathers to be read for instruction of newcomers: “For the sake of greater accuracy, I must add this too. There are other books, besides these, that are not included in the Canon. But the Fathers appointed them to be read by those who newly join us. These are people who want instruction in the teaching of godliness. The books are: the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the book called the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Shepherd.”

That list, written in 367, shows the breadth channel at work: not everyone could parse Origen, but everyone could hear the Shepherd read.

We would not want you to think the door was narrow when it was not.
